article.overview:
The Moon has no global magnetic field comparable with Earth's. It does have magnetised rocks in parts of its crust, and it is also moved by magnetic fields that come from outside, mainly from the solar wind. A magnetometer on the Moon can therefore measure three things: the local magnetism of the crust, the steady or slowly changing field at the surface, and the rapid changes that the solar wind causes. Each of these tells scientists something different about the Moon's interior and surface.

Two flown approaches are described here. In the first, a magnetometer on the surface records the field at one place for many years. The Apollo Lunar Surface Magnetometers (LSMs) of Apollo 12 and Apollo 16 are examples. In the second, a magnetometer in orbit maps the field over a larger area. Explorer 35, Lunar Prospector, Kaguya (SELENE) and ARTEMIS are examples. The Apollo 12 surface instrument measured a steady field of 36 ± 5 gamma at its site [1]. Lunar Prospector mapped crustal fields from orbit between January 1998 and July 1999 [3].
article.scope: Scope reading: this article covers the generic magnetometer class as a lunar instrument (measuring the magnetic field at the lunar surface or in lunar orbit). It describes flown examples: Apollo 12 and Apollo 16 surface magnetometers, the Apollo 16 portable magnetometer, Explorer 35, Lunar Prospector, Kaguya (SELENE) and ARTEMIS. Detailed sensing principles are cross-referenced, not repeated: fluxgate magnetometer (payload 013), vector magnetometer (payload 014) and scalar magnetometer (payload 015). Electromagnetic field sensors are payload 020.
article.description:
A magnetometer is an instrument that measures the strength and direction of a magnetic field. On a planetary body, the field has several sources. A permanent field can come from magnetised rocks in the crust. An induced field is created when a conducting interior responds to a changing external field, such as the solar wind. Some fields are very weak, so the instrument must be sensitive at the level of nanotesla or below. On the Moon, the field is measured in nanotesla (nT). One gamma is equal to one nanotesla, and the Apollo papers use gamma [1][2].

Lunar magnetometers have been of two broad types. Surface magnetometers are mounted on booms, sometimes on a tripod, and are powered and read out through the lander or central station. Orbital magnetometers are mounted on the spacecraft, usually on a long boom, so that the spacecraft's own magnetic field does not disturb the measurement. Most lunar magnetometers described in the sources read are fluxgate instruments, but the class also includes other sensing principles.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications:
The main purpose of a lunar magnetometer is to measure the magnetic field so that it can be separated into its sources. The Apollo 12 and 16 surface instruments were designed to measure both the magnitude and the time variations of the surface field. The aim was to learn about the Moon's internal electrical properties, including its electrical diffusivity, and to test whether a molten core exists [2].

The surface instruments also sought to determine the electrical conductivity and temperature of the lunar interior. The Apollo 12 analysis was based on the transient response of the surface field to changes in the solar-wind magnetic field. Simultaneous measurements from the orbiting Explorer 35 spacecraft were used for comparison [1]. The method depends on the time the interior takes to respond, so it probes how the interior conducts and how warm it is.

Orbital magnetometers map the crustal field. Lunar Prospector's stated objectives were to investigate the origin and nature of lunar crustal magnetic fields and to constrain the size of a metallic core [3]. Kaguya's magnetometer was intended to study the present and ancient magnetic and plasma environment of the Moon and to contribute to understanding its deep interior [5]. ARTEMIS carried particle and field instruments, including a fluxgate and a search-coil magnetometer, for use in lunar orbit [7].
article.operating_principle:
The surface and orbital magnetometers in this article use a fluxgate sensor, which is described in detail in payload 013. In brief, a magnetic core of high-permeability material is driven into saturation by an alternating current. The magnetic field being measured changes the way the core saturates, and the sensing winding picks up a second-harmonic signal whose size depends on the external field component along the sensor axis [2].

The Apollo 16 instrument description gives a clear example of this principle. Each sensor has a flattened toroidal permalloy core driven into saturation at 6000 Hz. The second harmonic of the drive frequency is generated in the sense winding with a magnitude proportional to the surface field. Its phase relative to the drive signal gives the field direction along the sensor axis. The output is amplified and synchronously demodulated before it is converted to digital form and transmitted [2].

Two other operating ideas matter for lunar measurements. Surface magnetometers use calibration flips. The Apollo 16 sensors could be rotated on gimbals to flip their measurement axes, which allowed calibration and a check on offsets [2]. Orbital magnetometers measure the spacecraft's own field as well as the external field, so the instrument is placed at the end of a boom. The Kaguya design used a 12 m mast for this reason [5].
article.scientific_importance:
Lunar magnetometers have shown that the Moon has crustal magnetism. This matters for the Moon's history, but the sources read do not settle how the crustal magnetism was produced. Apollo 12 and Apollo 16 surface data provided ground measurements at fixed sites, and Explorer 35 gave the orbital context for those records [1][2].

Orbital mapping adds spatial coverage. Lunar Prospector's stated objectives included the crustal field over the Moon and the induced dipole moment, which is linked to the size of a metallic core [3]. Kaguya provided calibrated magnetic-anomaly maps at 100 km and 30 km altitude [5]. ARTEMIS has measured fields in lunar orbit since 2011 [7].

Apollo's surface and orbital data together showed that the lunar magnetic environment changes with the solar wind. This makes a surface magnetometer valuable as a long-term monitoring instrument, because one station can record the same events repeatedly over many years [1][2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, range or power for a lunar magnetometer. The instruments below use different sensors, boom lengths, electronics and mission roles. physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: There is no single dimension set for a lunar magnetometer. The Apollo 12 LSM used three 100 cm booms with sensors 150 cm apart and 75 cm above the ground, and Table 1 of the 1971 memorandum (OCR) gives a 25 x 28 x 63 cm package. The Apollo 16 LSM used three 100 cm booms at 35 degrees to the horizontal, with sensors about 70 to 75 cm above the surface and about 150 cm apart. The Lunar Prospector MAG sensor is described as an 11 x 6.5 x 9 cm box. Kaguya's sensor sat at the end of a 12 m mast. Boom and package dimensions are not stated for ARTEMIS or for the Lunar Portable Magnetometer in the sources read. The proportions differ because the surface instruments needed booms to keep the sensors away from the electronics and the lander, and the orbital instruments needed a boom to keep the spacecraft field away from the sensor.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The two Apollo LSM packages are both recorded at 8.9 kg in the sources read: Table 1 of the Apollo 12 memorandum (read by OCR, so provisional) and the Apollo 16 instrument overview [1][2]. Mass is not stated for the Lunar Prospector MAG, Kaguya LMAG, ARTEMIS FGM or Explorer 35 magnetometers in the sources read. Mass determines launch and lander requirements, so these values are needed before any compatibility assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Apollo 16 LSM used 3.5 W average in daytime and 9.4 W at night. Table 1 of the Apollo 12 memorandum (OCR) gives 3.5 W in daytime and 7.5 W at night. The two night-time values differ and are reported as found. Power for the orbital instruments is not stated in the sources read. The Apollo 16 record also shows a thermal dependence of the sensor flip operation on temperature [2].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A lunar magnetometer must work in a severe thermal environment. The Apollo 16 record shows the problem clearly. The sensors could not complete all their flips at high noon temperatures in July 1972, and the z-axis data became static at low night temperatures in March 1975 [2]. The Apollo 12 design needed thermal changes before Apollo 15 and 16 [2]. Surface magnetometers therefore need thermal insulation, controlled heating and radiators, as well as a stable mounting.

The surface instruments must also be isolated from the magnetic field of the lander and the other experiments. The Apollo 12 design used long booms and separation for this reason [1]. Orbital instruments face the same issue in a different form. Kaguya's sensor was placed on a 12 m mast to keep the spacecraft field low at the sensor [5].

Measurement sensitivity needs a stable reference. Apollo 16 used gravity-level sensors to monitor sensor orientation to 0.2 degrees [2]. Offset stability is a separate issue. ARTEMIS sets a requirement of 0.2 nT per hour for the FGM [6].

Power and data rates are limited. The Apollo 16 LSM used 3.5 W in daytime and 9.4 W at night, with an average data rate of 116 bits per second [2]. Orbital instruments are usually limited by the spacecraft's power and telemetry budget, which the sources read do not quantify for each mission.
article.limitations:
A surface magnetometer records the field at one point. It cannot map the field over a region, and its results depend on the local geology and on the field from the lander. Orbital magnetometers map a larger area but at a larger distance from the sources, which limits the spatial resolution of the crustal field.

Separating the crustal field from the induced field is not simple. The Apollo 12 analysis used the transient response of the surface field to the solar wind, and it needed simultaneous orbital data for comparison [1]. A single surface instrument cannot separate these components by itself.

Surface instruments also have limited lifetimes. The Apollo 16 LSM lost data intermittently in 1973 and 1975 and was shut down in 1977 [2]. Lifetimes of orbital missions are set by the mission design and spacecraft health, and the sources read do not give these for all instruments.

The published specifications in this article are not directly comparable. The Apollo 12 and Apollo 16 LSMs use different ranges and resolutions, and the orbital instruments differ in boom length, sensor size and data products. No general accuracy figure is given for the class.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The transportation discussion separates surface magnetometers from orbital magnetometers. The Apollo surface instruments were set up by astronauts during extravehicular activity. The orbital examples were carried by spacecraft: Lunar Prospector, Kaguya and ARTEMIS. No lander or spacecraft compatibility is asserted.
transportation_process: Surface instruments (Apollo): the sources read do not describe stowage on the lunar module or release from it.
Surface instruments (Apollo): set up by astronauts during extravehicular activity; Apollo 12 activated 1969-11-19, Apollo 16 deployed 1972-04-21.
Orbital instruments (Lunar Prospector): launched 1998-01-06 from Cape Canaveral aboard an Athena 2; the sources read do not describe cruise, orbit insertion or boom commissioning in detail.
Orbital instruments (Kaguya): magnetometer on a 12 m mast extended from the spacecraft; launch and insertion details not described in the sources read.

Orbital instruments (ARTEMIS): two THEMIS spacecraft reassigned to the Moon in 2009; entered lunar orbit in June and July 2011 per NASA; boom deployment and commissioning not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo surface magnetometers were set up by astronauts during extravehicular activity. The sources read do not describe how the instruments were stowed on the lunar module or released from it. The Apollo 12 instrument was activated by Astronauts Conrad and Bean on 19 November 1969 [1]. The Apollo 16 LSM was deployed on 21 April 1972 [2]. Both instruments were part of the ALSEP, a set of experiments that the crew deployed on the surface. The Apollo deployment method is historical. It is not evidence of how a new surface magnetometer would be delivered. Any future surface magnetometer would need a stowage, release and deployment design to suit the lander and the mission, and that design is not described in the sources read. Lunar Prospector launched on 6 January 1998 from Cape Canaveral aboard an Athena 2 rocket [4]. Its magnetometer shares an electronics box with the Electron Reflectometer, and the combined instrument operated in lunar orbit until the planned end on 31 July 1999 [3][4]. The sources read do not describe the spacecraft's integration, cruise or orbit-insertion sequence for the magnetometer in detail. ARTEMIS reused two THEMIS spacecraft after they were reassigned to the Moon in 2009. The two spacecraft entered lunar orbit in June and July 2011 [7]. The sources read do not describe the magnetometer boom deployment or the commissioning sequence. The Kaguya magnetometer was placed on a 12 m mast extended from the spacecraft [5]. Its launch and orbit-insertion details are not described in the sources read.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 12 and Apollo 16 LSMs (surface), the Apollo 16 LPM (portable surface), Explorer 35 (early lunar orbit), Lunar Prospector (1998-1999), Kaguya (2007-2009) and ARTEMIS (from 2011) are the flown examples in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility is asserted with any named lander, rover or spacecraft. The sources read describe the flown instruments and their own spacecraft, but they do not establish compatibility with any future lander or spacecraft. Any future assessment would need the instrument's mass, dimensions, mounting interface, thermal requirements, power, data rate and deployment method.

article.historical_significance:
The Apollo 12 magnetometer reported a steady field of 36 ± 5 gamma at its surface site [1]. The Apollo 16 LSM was part of a surface network with the Apollo 12 and Apollo 15 instruments, according to the Apollo 16 instrument overview [2]. Those surface records combined with orbital observations were used to study the Moon's electrical and thermal interior.

Explorer 35 gave orbital magnetic-field observations while the Apollo surface instruments were operating [2]. Lunar Prospector mapped the crustal field from orbit in 1998 and 1999 [3]. Kaguya extended this with a calibrated time series and anomaly maps [5]. ARTEMIS used fluxgate instruments in lunar orbit from 2011, in a plasma and solar-wind study [7].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties:
- - Apollo 12 and 16 values. The Apollo 12 mass, dimensions and night-time power are read from OCR text of a 1971 memorandum. Treat them as provisional [1].
- - Apollo 15 network. The Apollo 16 instrument overview lists the network as Apollo 12, 15 and 16 [2]. A secondary summary lists Apollo 12, 14 and 16 instead. The Apollo 15 surface instrument was not described.
- - Apollo 16 image identifications. The LSM and LPM identifications for the two Apollo 16 frames rely on secondary catalogue descriptions. The NASA catalogue pages for those frames could not be located.
- - Lunar Prospector. Boom length, mass and power are not stated on the ODE page. The PI and co-investigators are not identified in the sources read. The impact outcome is not verified in the primary sources read.
- - Kaguya. The JAXA equipment page did not resolve. Mass, power, range, PI and dates are unverified, and the 2007 launch and June 2009 end come from a secondary summary. The 2009 in-orbit calibration paper was not read.
- - ARTEMIS. NASA's page gives the 2011 lunar-orbit dates, but the operating status is not confirmed after the 2017 statement on the page. The FGM offset-stability statement applies to the THEMIS near-Earth phase.
- - Explorer 35. Magnetometer specifications and the NSSDC experiment records were not read.
- - Apollo 15 and 16 subsatellite magnetometers. Described only in search summaries of later papers. Not described in this article.
- - Remanent-field values. Search summaries cite remanent-field values for the Apollo 15 and 16 sites. The primary paper was not read, so no values are used here.
- - Soviet and other national instruments. Not researched.
- - Sensing principle. The fluxgate physics is in payload 013. The vector and scalar sensing approaches are in payloads 014 and 015. Other principles were not reviewed in this article.
- - Lunar landing sites. This article does not recommend lunar landing sites or locations. That is deferred by the user.

data_quality_notes: Scope: class-level article (generic lunar magnetometer) with flown examples. Fluxgate, vector and scalar sensing physics are cross-referenced to payloads 013, 014 and 015 and not repeated; electromagnetic field sensors are payload 020.

Apollo 12 LSM mass (8.9 kg), dimensions (25 x 28 x 63 cm), power (3.5 W day, 7.5 W night) and operating temperature come from Table 1 of NASA TM X-62,012, read by OCR. Treat as provisional. The mass matches the Apollo 16 figure exactly, which should be checked against the original scan.

Apollo 12 range (0 to ±400 gamma, 0.2 gamma resolution) is from the memorandum text, while Table 1 OCR lists 400/200/100 gamma; Apollo 16 range (±50/100/200, 0.1 gamma) is from the PDS document. The two configurations are not directly comparable.
Night-time power conflict between sources: Apollo 12 Table 1 (OCR) gives 7.5 W and Apollo 16 gives 9.4 W. Both are reported as found.
Apollo network membership conflict: the Apollo 16 PDS document lists Apollo 12, 15 and 16; a secondary summary lists 12, 14 and 16. The Apollo 15 surface instrument was not described.
